story.tagline: A grief the Mughals decided to build in marble.
story.intro: The Taj Mahal is the tomb Shah Jahan raised for his wife Mumtaz Mahal on the right bank of the Yamuna at Agra. It is not one building but a complete walled complex — gateway, mosque, guest hall, and a four-part garden — arranged so that the mausoleum is the only thing that ever stands at the centre of the view. UNESCO inscribed it in 1983.
story.history: Mumtaz Mahal died in 1631 at Burhanpur giving birth to her fourteenth child. Work on the tomb began at Agra the following year and the mausoleum itself was substantially complete by about 1643, with the wider complex finished around 1653. Ustad Ahmad Lahauri is the name most often attached to the design. The white marble came from Makrana in Rajasthan, and the inlaid flowers use jasper, jade, carnelian and lapis lazuli brought from across Asia. Shah Jahan was deposed by his son Aurangzeb in 1658 and spent his last years at Agra Fort; he is buried beside his wife in the crypt.

visiting.bestTime: October to March, and go at sunrise
visiting.hours: Sunrise to sunset; closed Fridays. Night viewing on five nights around the full moon
visiting.entry: ₹50 Indians · ₹540 SAARC and BIMSTEC · ₹1,100 foreign nationals; add ₹200 to step onto the mausoleum platform
visiting.duration: 2–3 hours
visiting.nearestAirport: Agra (AGR), 13 km; most travellers fly to Delhi

seeThis.title: The optical trick at the gate
seeThis.detail: Frame the Taj in the great gateway's arch and walk forward. The building appears to shrink as you approach — the arch is doing the work, and it is the one photograph everyone gets wrong by rushing.

seeThis.title: Pietra dura, up close
seeThis.detail: The flowers on the plinth walls are not painted. Each petal is a separate sliver of stone cut to fit. Put a torch against one and the carnelian glows red.

seeThis.title: The two cenotaphs
seeThis.detail: Mumtaz Mahal's cenotaph sits dead centre; Shah Jahan's was added later, larger and off-axis — the single asymmetry in an otherwise perfectly balanced building.

seeThis.title: Mehtab Bagh across the river
seeThis.detail: The Moonlight Garden on the far bank lines up exactly with the mausoleum. It is where the complex was meant to be seen from at dusk, and it is nearly empty.

tips: Tickets are timed and cheaper booked online through the ASI portal; the ₹200 mausoleum supplement is a separate stub — keep it, they check at the steps.
Tripods, food and anything larger than a small bag are refused at the gate, and there is no cloakroom worth the queue. Travel light.
Fridays are closed for prayers, so a Friday in Agra is best spent at Agra Fort and Itimad-ud-Daulah instead.

story.tagline: A city that has never stopped being itself.
story.intro: Varanasi runs along a four-kilometre curve of the Ganga in Uttar Pradesh, and almost everything that matters happens on the water's edge. Some eighty-odd ghats step down to the river; pilgrims bathe at dawn, cremations burn without pause at two of them, and the whole city turns out for the aarti at dusk. Hindus know it as Kashi, the city of light.
story.history: Settlement here goes back to at least the first millennium BCE, which makes Varanasi one of the oldest continuously lived-in cities anywhere. The Buddha gave his first sermon at Sarnath, ten kilometres north, in the fifth century BCE. The present Kashi Vishwanath temple was rebuilt in 1780 by Ahilyabai Holkar of Indore after earlier temples on the site were destroyed; the gold plating on its spires was Maharaja Ranjit Singh's gift in the 1830s. Most of the stone ghats you walk on today were built or rebuilt in the eighteenth century by Maratha rulers — the Scindias, Holkars and Peshwas each left one.

visiting.bestTime: October to March; Dev Deepawali in November is extraordinary
visiting.hours: The ghats never close. Ganga aarti at Dashashwamedh begins around dusk, roughly 6:30 pm in winter
visiting.entry: Free; a shared sunrise boat is about ₹150–300 per person
visiting.duration: Two days at minimum — one dawn, one dusk
visiting.nearestStation: Varanasi Junction (Cantt), 5 km from the ghats

seeThis.title: The river at first light
seeThis.detail: Take a boat at 5:30 am and let it drift north to south. The whole city faces east, so sunrise hits every ghat at once — this is the view the old lithographs were drawn from.

seeThis.title: Ganga aarti at Dashashwamedh
seeThis.detail: Seven priests, brass lamps the size of a torso, and a crowd of thousands. Arrive an hour early for a step, or watch it from a moored boat.

seeThis.title: Manikarnika, respectfully
seeThis.detail: The main cremation ghat burns around the clock. Photography is genuinely unwelcome here; stand back, watch, and put the phone away.

seeThis.title: The lanes behind the ghats
seeThis.detail: Gullies barely a shoulder wide connect the riverfront to Vishwanath Gali — silk shops, kachori stalls, and a temple every fifty metres. Getting lost is the point.

tips: Boatmen quote per boat, not per head — settle the number and the route before you push off, and pay at the end.
The Kashi Vishwanath corridor has airport-style security: no phones, no leather, no bags. Leave everything at a locker on the approach.
Banarasi silk is sold everywhere and woven in far fewer places. If a shop offers a rickshaw ride to a 'government emporium', it is a commission run.

name: Jaipur
description: India's first planned city, with Amber Fort on the ridge above it.
panoramaCredit: Udaiveer — CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

panoramas.label: Birla Auditorium forecourt, Jaipur
panoramas.credit: Udaiveer — CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

story.tagline: A city laid out on a grid three centuries before anyone called it urban planning.
story.intro: Jaipur was built from nothing in 1727 when Sawai Jai Singh II moved his capital down from the hills at Amber. What he commissioned was a walled city on a nine-block grid, with streets of a fixed width and shopfronts of a fixed height — the first planned city in India, and still legible as one. The old city was inscribed by UNESCO in 2019.
story.history: Jai Singh II was an astronomer as much as a ruler, and it shows. His architect Vidyadhar Bhattacharya laid the city out on principles from the Shilpa Shastra, and Jai Singh built the Jantar Mantar observatory beside his palace in 1734 — nineteen masonry instruments, including the Vrihat Samrat Yantra, a sundial twenty-seven metres tall that still keeps time to about two seconds. Amber Fort, on the ridge nine kilometres north, is older: Raja Man Singh I began the present palace in 1592 on the site of an earlier Meena fort. The Hawa Mahal came in 1799, built by Sawai Pratap Singh so the women of the court could watch the street through its 953 windows without being seen. The pink wash that gives the city its nickname was applied in 1876 to welcome the Prince of Wales.

visiting.hours: Amber Fort 8 am–5:30 pm; Hawa Mahal 9 am–4:30 pm; Jantar Mantar 9 am–4:30 pm
visiting.entry: Amber Fort ₹100 · ₹500 foreign nationals. Hawa Mahal ₹50 · ₹200. Jantar Mantar ₹50 · ₹200
visiting.duration: Two full days for the old city and Amber

seeThis.title: Sheesh Mahal at Amber
seeThis.detail: The mirror hall was built so that a single candle would read as a night sky. Guides will demonstrate; it works.

seeThis.title: Ganesh Pol
seeThis.detail: The painted gate into the private palace at Amber — frescoed in mineral colours that have never been repainted, only cleaned.

seeThis.title: The Vrihat Samrat Yantra
seeThis.detail: At Jantar Mantar, watch the shadow edge move down the marble quadrant. You can see it travel, which is the whole point of building a sundial this large.

seeThis.title: Hawa Mahal from inside
seeThis.detail: Everyone photographs the honeycomb facade from the road. Go in and climb to the top floor — the windows are shallow alcoves, and the breeze through them is the reason for the name.

tips: Amber Fort's elephant rides are capped and heavily queued; the jeep up the same ramp costs less and starts moving immediately.
A composite ticket covers Amber, Jantar Mantar, Hawa Mahal, Nahargarh and Albert Hall for two days — worth it if you are seeing three or more.
Sunset from Nahargarh Fort looks straight down onto the grid Jai Singh drew. Go up at about 5 pm and stay.

name: Kerala Backwaters
description: A lagoon network of lakes and canals behind the Malabar coast.
panoramaCredit: Anil R.V — CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

panoramas.label: Vellayani Lake, Thiruvananthapuram
panoramas.credit: Anil R.V — CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

story.tagline: Nine hundred kilometres of water where the road would be.
story.intro: The backwaters are a chain of brackish lagoons and canals running parallel to the Arabian Sea for most of Kerala's length, fed by dozens of rivers and separated from the ocean by a thin barrier of sand. Vembanad, the largest lake in India, sits at the centre of the system. Villages here are strung along the banks, and for many of them the canal is still the main road.
story.history: The backwaters were a working freight network long before they were a holiday. Rice, coir and spices moved along them in kettuvallams — long cargo boats stitched together with coir rope and no nails at all, some of them thirty metres from end to end. When lorries took the freight in the twentieth century the boats went idle, and from the 1990s they were converted into the houseboats now moored at Alappuzha. Inland, Kuttanad is one of very few places on earth where farming is done below sea level: paddy fields sit up to two metres beneath the water line, protected by bunds and drained by pumps, a system worked out in the nineteenth century.

visiting.bestTime: September to March; the Nehru Trophy Boat Race is the second Saturday of August
visiting.hours: Houseboats board around noon and disembark the next morning at nine
visiting.entry: Free to travel the waterways; a shared shikara hour is about ₹500, an overnight houseboat from roughly ₹7,000
visiting.duration: One overnight, or a half-day canoe if time is short
visiting.nearestStation: Alappuzha, 3 km from the boat jetty

seeThis.title: The narrow canals, not the lake
seeThis.detail: Big houseboats are confined to wide water. Take a canoe into the village canals around Kainakary and you pass through people's back gardens.

seeThis.title: Chinese fishing nets
seeThis.detail: Cantilevered shore nets, worked by four men and a stone counterweight. They line the Kochi waterfront and turn up along the northern backwaters.

seeThis.title: Kuttanad's bunds
seeThis.detail: Walk a paddy bund and look down — the field is below the level of the canal beside you. The pumps run day and night.

seeThis.title: Toddy shops on the bank
seeThis.detail: Unmarked sheds serving fermented palm sap and hard-fried karimeen. The food is the reason to stop.

tips: Overnight houseboats stop cruising at sunset by law and moor for the night, so pay for the route rather than the hours.
Alappuzha is the busy hub; Kumarakom on the eastern shore of Vembanad is quieter, and Munroe Island quieter still.
The mosquitoes at dusk are serious. Repellent matters more than a good camera here.

name: Ladakh
description: High-altitude monasteries and cold desert between the Himalaya and Karakoram.
panoramaCredit: Aman Gujar — CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

panoramas.label: Hemis Monastery courtyard
panoramas.credit: Aman Gujar — CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

story.tagline: Above the tree line, where the sky does most of the work.
story.intro: Ladakh is a cold desert on the Tibetan plateau's western edge, held between the Himalaya and the Karakoram. Leh, the main town, sits at about 3,500 metres; the passes and lakes beyond it run higher still. Almost nothing grows without irrigation, so villages are green threads along meltwater channels, and the monasteries stand on the dry rock above them.
story.history: Ladakh was an independent Buddhist kingdom from the tenth century, ruled from Shey and later Leh by the Namgyal dynasty, and it grew rich on the trade between Kashmir, Tibet and Central Asia. Hemis, the largest and wealthiest monastery in Ladakh, belongs to the Drukpa lineage and was re-established in 1672 under King Sengge Namgyal; its Hemis Tsechu masked-dance festival still fills the courtyard every summer. Ladakh was annexed by the Dogras of Jammu in the 1830s and joined the state of Jammu and Kashmir; it became a separate union territory of India in 2019.

visiting.bestTime: June to September; the road passes are shut by snow the rest of the year
visiting.hours: Monasteries generally 8 am–1 pm and 2–6 pm
visiting.entry: Hemis ₹100. An Inner Line Permit — about ₹400 plus a daily fee — is required for Nubra, Pangong and Tso Moriri
visiting.duration: Seven days minimum, including two to acclimatise
visiting.nearestStation: Jammu Tawi, 700 km — everyone flies or drives

seeThis.title: Hemis in June
seeThis.detail: The Tsechu fills the courtyard with cham dancers in silk and painted masks. Every second year a thangka the height of the building is unrolled down the wall.

seeThis.title: Thiksey at dawn prayers
seeThis.detail: Twelve tiers of whitewashed buildings on a hill, laid out like a smaller Potala. Prayers start about 6:30 am and visitors are welcome to sit at the back.

seeThis.title: The Maitreya at Diskit
seeThis.detail: A thirty-two-metre seated Buddha facing north up the Shyok toward Pakistan, finished in 2010 and visible from most of Nubra.

seeThis.title: Pangong Tso's colour
seeThis.detail: The lake sits at 4,350 metres and changes from turquoise to near-black through the day. Two-thirds of it lies in Tibet.

tips: Give yourself two full days in Leh doing nothing before going higher. Altitude sickness at 5,000 metres is a genuine medical emergency, not an inconvenience.
Mobile data works only on postpaid Indian connections in Ladakh, and barely outside Leh. Download maps before you leave town.
Carry cash. ATMs cluster in Leh and are unreliable everywhere else.

name: Goa
description: Beaches, Konkan temples and four centuries of Portuguese building.
panoramaCredit: Rakesh92c — CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

panoramas.label: Mahalasa Narayani temple, Mardol
panoramas.credit: Rakesh92c — CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

story.tagline: Two coastlines in one state — the beach one, and the older one inland.
story.intro: Goa is India's smallest state, a hundred kilometres of Konkan coast with a laterite hinterland of paddy, spice gardens and rivers behind it. The beaches from Candolim to Anjuna carry the reputation, but the interior — Old Goa's basilicas, the Ponda temples, the Western Ghats at Dudhsagar — is where the state's four hundred years of layered history actually sits.
story.history: The Portuguese took Goa in 1510 under Afonso de Albuquerque and held it until Indian forces entered in December 1961 — a longer European presence than anywhere else in Asia. Old Goa was the capital until cholera and malaria emptied it in the seventeenth century; the Basilica of Bom Jesus, built between 1594 and 1605, survives from that city and holds the relics of St Francis Xavier, put on public view roughly once a decade. The churches and convents of Old Goa were inscribed by UNESCO in 1986. Hindu temples in the Ponda taluka, including Mahalasa at Mardol, were rebuilt there in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries after deities were carried inland out of Portuguese-controlled territory — which is why they look like nothing else in India, with lamp towers and pitched Konkan roofs.

visiting.bestTime: November to February; the monsoon from June to September is dramatic and cheap
visiting.hours: Basilica of Bom Jesus 9 am–6:30 pm; beaches always
visiting.entry: Free at the churches and the beaches; Dudhsagar jeep safari about ₹400
visiting.duration: Four to five days
visiting.nearestAirport: Manohar International, Mopa (GOX) in the north; Dabolim (GOI) in the south
visiting.nearestStation: Madgaon for the south, Thivim for the north

seeThis.title: Bom Jesus's laterite facade
seeThis.detail: The exterior plaster was stripped in 1950 and never replaced, so the basilica is raw red stone — unlike every other church in Old Goa.

seeThis.title: The Ponda temple lamp towers
seeThis.detail: Multi-storeyed deepstambhas that are lit on festival nights. Mahalasa's is the finest, and its brass Garuda pillar is unique in Goa.

seeThis.title: Fontainhas, Panaji
seeThis.detail: The Latin Quarter — ochre and indigo houses, azulejo street signs, and an ordinance requiring owners to repaint after every monsoon.

seeThis.title: A beach shack at low tide
seeThis.detail: Palolem and Agonda in the south still have the version with plastic chairs, a kitchen behind, and grilled kingfish.

tips: Rent a scooter — Goa is spread out, buses are slow, and taxis here are notoriously expensive and unmetered.
Old Goa is best at 9 am. Coach parties arrive by eleven and the basilica interior gets very full.
Feni is a local spirit made from cashew apple or coconut sap and does not travel legally out of state. Drink it where it is made.

name: Qutub Minar, Delhi
description: The tallest brick minaret in the world, and the ruins around its foot.
panoramaCredit: Samthe030601 — CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

panoramas.label: Inside the Quwwat-ul-Islam courtyard
panoramas.credit: Samthe030601 — CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

panoramas.label: The complex from outside the colonnade
panoramas.credit: Samthe030601 — CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

story.tagline: Delhi's first skyscraper, and it is eight hundred years old.
story.intro: The Qutub Minar stands 72.5 metres above the Mehrauli ruins in south Delhi — five tapering storeys of red sandstone and marble, fluted and banded with Quranic inscription. Around it lies the Qutb complex: the earliest surviving mosque in northern India, a fourth-century iron pillar that has barely rusted, tombs, a madrasa, and the stump of a second tower that was meant to be twice as tall. UNESCO inscribed the complex in 1993.
story.history: Qutb al-Din Aibak began the minaret in 1199, the year after he took Delhi, and completed only the first storey. Iltutmish added three more by about 1220, and Firoz Shah Tughlaq rebuilt the top after lightning damage in 1369 — which is why the upper storeys are marble and the lower ones are not. The Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque beside it was raised from 1192 using columns taken from twenty-seven earlier temples; you can still read the carved figures on them. The Iron Pillar in the courtyard is older than everything around it: a Gupta-period column of the fourth or fifth century, nearly seven and a quarter metres tall, whose phosphorus-rich iron has resisted corrosion for sixteen hundred years. Alauddin Khalji started the Alai Minar in 1311 intending to double the Qutub's height; he died with 25 metres built, and it was abandoned.

visiting.bestTime: October to March; go late afternoon for the light on the sandstone
visiting.entry: ₹40 · ₹600 foreign nationals; ₹35 and ₹550 if booked online
visiting.duration: 1.5–2 hours
visiting.nearestStation: Qutab Minar metro on the Yellow Line, 1.5 km

seeThis.title: The reused temple columns
seeThis.detail: Walk the mosque colonnade and look up. Bells, garlands and defaced figures — twelfth-century builders repurposing what was already on the site, and not hiding it.

seeThis.title: The Iron Pillar
seeThis.detail: Sixteen centuries in the open Delhi air with almost no rust. Metallurgists still cite it; the railing went up because visitors kept trying to encircle it.

seeThis.title: Alai Darwaza
seeThis.detail: Alauddin Khalji's 1311 gateway is the first true dome and true arch built in India, and it is the most refined thing in the complex.

seeThis.title: The unfinished Alai Minar
seeThis.detail: A rubble core 25 metres high behind the mosque. Standing at its base tells you exactly how ambitious the plan was.

tips: Climbing the minaret has been closed to the public since a stairwell crush in 1981. No guide can get you in.
The Mehrauli Archaeological Park next door has Balban's tomb, Jamali Kamali and the Rajon ki Baoli — all free, and almost empty.
The complex is at its best about an hour before closing, when the low sun makes the inscription bands stand out.

story.tagline: They started at the top of the hill and cut downwards.
story.intro: Ellora is a two-kilometre line of basalt cliff near Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar in Maharashtra, hollowed out into thirty-four monasteries and temples between about the sixth and tenth centuries. Twelve are Buddhist, seventeen Hindu and five Jain, and they were excavated alongside each other rather than in sequence — which is the most interesting fact about the site. UNESCO inscribed it in 1983.
story.history: The caves sit on an old trade route between the Deccan and the western ports, which paid for them. The Buddhist group in the south is the earliest, from roughly the sixth to eighth centuries, and includes Cave 10 — the Vishvakarma chaitya, the only Buddhist prayer hall at Ellora, with a stone vault carved to imitate wooden ribs. The Hindu caves belong mainly to the Kalachuri and Rashtrakuta periods. Cave 16, the Kailasa temple, was begun in the eighth century under the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I and is the largest monolithic structure anywhere: workers removed something like 200,000 tonnes of rock, cutting from the top down and inwards, and produced a full free-standing temple with courtyard, gateway and elephants — with no possibility of correcting a mistake. The Jain caves at the northern end came last, in the ninth and tenth centuries.

visiting.entry: ₹40 · ₹600 foreign nationals
visiting.duration: Half a day; a full day if you also want Ajanta light

seeThis.title: Kailasa from the cliff path
seeThis.detail: There is a track up the rock face to the south. From the top you look down into the temple and finally understand that it is a hole, not a building.

seeThis.title: Cave 10's ribbed vault
seeThis.detail: Stone carved to look like curved timber beams, because that is what the builders' earlier wooden halls were made of. The acoustics under it are extraordinary.

seeThis.title: Cave 12, all three floors
seeThis.detail: A three-storey monastery — the Teen Thal — with rows of seated Buddhas on the top floor and monks' cells below.

seeThis.title: The Jain Indra Sabha
seeThis.detail: Cave 32 at the far north end, with traces of the original painted ceiling still readable. Almost nobody walks that far.

tips: Closed Tuesdays; Ajanta closes Mondays. Plan two consecutive days and you can do both.

story.tagline: A temple with a city built around it, rather than the other way round.
story.intro: The Meenakshi Sundareswarar temple occupies six hectares in the middle of Madurai, and the old city's streets run in concentric squares around it. Fourteen gopurams — gateway towers crusted with painted stucco figures — rise over the walls, the tallest of them about 52 metres. The goddess Meenakshi is the principal deity here, and her shrine takes precedence over her consort Sundareswarar's, which is unusual.
story.history: Madurai was the Pandya capital and is referred to in Tamil Sangam literature more than two thousand years ago. The temple as it now stands is largely a rebuilding: the earlier complex was sacked by Malik Kafur's forces in 1310, and reconstruction was carried out under the Nayak rulers of Madurai in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, above all under Thirumalai Nayak, who ruled from 1623 to 1659. He also built the palace a kilometre southeast — its surviving courtyard, ringed by twenty-metre granite columns under a stucco dome, is about a quarter of what once stood there. The temple's gopuram figures are repainted roughly every twelve years in the Kumbhabhishekam ritual, which is why they look startlingly bright.

Phones and cameras are not allowed inside. There are deposit counters at the East Gate.

story.tagline: Two thousand two hundred years old, and the gateways still tell the whole story.
story.intro: Sanchi is a hilltop of stupas, temples and monastery foundations rising above the plain in Raisen district, Madhya Pradesh. The Great Stupa at its centre is the oldest stone structure in India still standing. What makes the site remarkable is the four gateways around it: torana arches carved end to end with scenes from the Buddha's lives, told entirely without showing the Buddha himself. UNESCO inscribed Sanchi in 1989.
story.history: The emperor Ashoka founded the first stupa here in the third century BCE, a brick dome over relics, and raised a polished sandstone pillar beside it. In the second and first centuries BCE the Shungas encased the dome in stone and doubled its size to the 36 metres across it is today, and added the railing and the terrace. The four toranas were carved around the first century BCE, in the Satavahana period, and paid for by donors — merchants, guilds, monks and nuns — whose names are inscribed on them. Sanchi has no direct connection to events in the Buddha's life, which is probably why it was never a target: it faded quietly as Buddhism declined in India and was forgotten until a British officer, Henry Taylor, recorded it in 1818. Careless early excavation did real damage; John Marshall's restoration between 1912 and 1919 is what you walk through now.

story.tagline: Lost in the forest for a thousand years, and the paint survived it.
story.intro: Ajanta is a horseshoe-shaped gorge on the Waghora river in Aurangabad district, Maharashtra, with thirty Buddhist caves cut into the inside of the curve. Some are chaityas — prayer halls with a stupa at the end — and the rest viharas, monasteries with cells around a central court. What separates Ajanta from every other cave site is the painting: large stretches of fifth-century mural survive on the walls and ceilings. UNESCO inscribed it in 1983.
story.history: The caves were cut in two widely separated phases. The earlier group belongs to the Satavahana period, roughly the second century BCE to the first century CE, and is austere. The second phase came under the Vakataka king Harishena in the second half of the fifth century, and produced almost everything that makes Ajanta famous — Caves 1, 2, 16, 17, 19 and 26, their sculpture and their paintings. Work stopped abruptly, probably when Harishena's dynasty collapsed, leaving several caves unfinished mid-chisel. The monks left, the forest closed in, and the site was not seen again until 1819, when a British officer named John Smith, out hunting tiger, spotted an arch above the undergrowth and scratched his name on a pillar in Cave 10. It is still there.

story.tagline: Built to welcome an emperor, remembered for watching the last of them leave.
story.intro: The Gateway of India is a 26-metre basalt arch on the Colaba waterfront, facing the harbour. It is Mumbai's most recognisable structure and the city's default meeting point — ferries to Elephanta leave from the steps beside it, and the Taj Mahal Palace hotel stands directly opposite.
story.history: The arch was proposed to commemorate the landing of George V and Queen Mary at Apollo Bunder in December 1911 — they saw only a cardboard mock-up. George Wittet designed the permanent structure in an Indo-Saracenic manner, borrowing from sixteenth-century Gujarati architecture; the foundation was laid in 1920 and the Gateway opened in 1924. Its most quoted moment is the opposite of its purpose: in February 1948 the First Battalion of the Somerset Light Infantry marched through it to their ships, the last British troops to leave India. The Taj Mahal Palace behind it is older, opened in 1903 by Jamsetji Tata, and was one of the buildings attacked in November 2008.

story.tagline: The Pallavas carved a port town out of granite and left it facing the sea.
story.intro: Mahabalipuram — Mamallapuram — sits 55 kilometres south of Chennai on the Coromandel coast. Its monuments are almost all cut from the granite outcrops that run through the town: monolithic shrines, cave temples, and one enormous open-air relief. The Shore Temple is the exception, built from dressed blocks right at the waterline. UNESCO inscribed the group in 1984.
story.history: This was a Pallava port from the seventh century, trading with Southeast Asia — which is part of why Pallava temple forms turn up later in Cambodia and Java. Most of the rock-cut work belongs to the reigns of Mahendravarman I and Narasimhavarman I (Mamalla), after whom the town is named. The Shore Temple came a little later, around 700 to 728, under Narasimhavarman II; it is one of the earliest structural stone temples in south India, and centuries of salt wind have rounded its carving. The Pancha Rathas — five shrines, each cut whole from a single boulder in a different architectural style — were never finished or consecrated, which is exactly what makes them useful: they are a builder's sample book. In December 2004 the tsunami briefly pulled the water back and exposed submerged masonry offshore, supporting the old local account of seven temples of which only one remained.

visiting.bestTime: November to February; the dance festival runs December to January
visiting.entry: ₹40 · ₹600 foreign nationals — one ticket covers the Shore Temple and the Pancha Rathas
visiting.duration: Half a day

seeThis.title: The Pancha Rathas
seeThis.detail: Five monolithic shrines in five different styles, each carved top-down out of one rock. Draupadi's is a thatched hut in granite.

seeThis.title: The Shore Temple at sunrise

seeThis.title: Krishna's Butter Ball
seeThis.detail: A six-metre granite boulder resting on a slope at an angle that should not hold. It has held for well over a thousand years.

Stone carving is still a living trade here — the workshops along the main road are working craftsmen, not souvenir stalls.
Combine it with Dakshinachitra on the drive back to Chennai; the East Coast Road makes it easy.

story.tagline: Two thousand years old, cut by traders, and still on the trade route.
story.intro: A cluster of early Buddhist cave complexes sits in the hills either side of the Bhor Ghat, between Mumbai and Pune. Karla holds the largest and best-preserved chaitya hall in India; Bhaja, Bedse and Kondana are smaller and older. All four look down on the pass that carried goods between the Deccan plateau and the Konkan ports — which is exactly who paid for them.
story.history: Bhaja is the earliest, cut in the second century BCE, and its chaitya still shows sockets where a wooden facade was fixed to the rock. Karla's Great Chaitya followed around 120 CE under Satavahana rule: 45 metres deep, with 37 octagonal columns, a stupa at the apse, and a stone vault ribbed in teak — some of the original timber is still in place after nineteen centuries, which makes it among the oldest structural wood surviving anywhere. Inscriptions on the pillars name the donors: merchants, bankers and guilds from Nashik and Junnar, and in several cases Yavanas — Greeks settled in western India. Bedse, first century BCE, has bell-shaped capitals carrying carved riders. The complexes were monastic rest houses as much as temples, sited a day's travel apart along the road.

story.tagline: Half demolished before anyone realised what it was.
story.intro: The Currency Building stands on Dalhousie Square — officially B. B. D. Bagh — in the administrative heart of old Calcutta. Three storeys of red brick with Venetian arcaded windows and a triple-domed central hall, it is now an exhibition space run by the Archaeological Survey of India, and one of the more unexpected things to walk into in central Kolkata.
story.history: The building went up in 1833 for the Agra Bank, and from 1868 the Government of India used it as its currency office — issuing and later destroying paper money, which is where the name comes from. It was abandoned in the twentieth century and by 1994 demolition was under way; the domes had already been taken down when the ASI intervened and had it declared a protected monument in 1998. Restoration ran for the better part of two decades, and the building reopened as a gallery and exhibition venue in January 2020. Dalhousie Square around it is one of the densest surviving colonial-era ensembles anywhere in Asia — the Writers' Building, the GPO on the site of the old Fort William, St Andrew's Kirk — and the whole square has been listed by the World Monuments Fund as endangered.

story.tagline: Ajanta's crowds are two hours away. These caves get about nine visitors an hour.
story.intro: Twelve rock-cut Buddhist caves sit in two groups on a ridge north of Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, a couple of kilometres uphill from Bibi ka Maqbara. They are cut into softer trap rock than Ajanta and Ellora, so the carving has weathered — but the sculpture in the later caves is some of the most accomplished Vajrayana work in the Deccan, and you will usually have it to yourself.
story.history: The caves span roughly the second to the eighth centuries CE. Cave 4, the only chaitya hall in the group, is the earliest — a modest apsidal prayer hall of about the second century, contemporary with the Satavahana work at Karla. The rest are viharas of the sixth and seventh centuries, when the Kalachuris and then the Chalukyas held the region, and they belong to the same wave of patronage that produced the later caves at Ajanta. Cave 7 is the one worth the climb: a shrine surrounded by large panels of bodhisattvas and female figures, including a much-photographed dancing scene with musicians, and litany panels showing Avalokiteshvara delivering worshippers from eight named perils. The site sits on the ancient route between Pratishthana, the Satavahana capital, and the western ports.

seeThis.title: The litany of Avalokiteshvara
seeThis.detail: Panels showing the bodhisattva rescuing travellers from shipwreck, fire, bandits and elephants — a merchant's anxieties, carved for merchants.

Bring a torch. The shrines are unlit and Cave 7's best panels are in deep shadow.

story.tagline: A monastery paid for by the traffic on the road below.
story.intro: Twenty-four rock-cut caves stand in a line on the Trirashmi hill, about eight kilometres south of Nashik. They are Buddhist, they are early, and they are the reason a lot of what we know about the Satavahana and Western Kshatrapa dynasties is known at all — the inscriptions cut into their walls are among the most-quoted historical documents of the Deccan. Locally they are the Pandavleni, the Pandavas' caves, though the Pandavas have nothing to do with them.
story.history: Excavation ran from roughly the first century BCE into the third century CE, in a period when the hill overlooked one of the busiest trade routes between the Deccan plateau and the western coast. The caves are viharas — monks' residences — with one chaitya prayer hall, Cave 18. Cave 3 and Cave 10 are the two great viharas: Cave 3 was given by Gautami Balashri, mother of the Satavahana king Gautamiputra Satakarni, and its inscription is effectively that king's obituary; Cave 10 was cut in the time of the Kshatrapa ruler Nahapana and carries donative records from his son-in-law Ushavadata. The later caves show Mahayana images, the standing and seated Buddhas that were added as the doctrine changed around them.

visiting.duration: Two to three hours, including the climb

seeThis.detail: About twenty minutes of steps from the car park. There is a viewpoint most of the way up where the whole Nashik plain opens out behind you.

seeThis.title: Cave 3's donor inscription
seeThis.detail: Cut across the verandah wall. It is the record of Gautami Balashri praising her son, and historians have been arguing about its dating for over a century.

seeThis.title: Cave 18, the chaitya
seeThis.detail: The only prayer hall on the hill, with a carved facade imitating a timber-framed window. Everything else here is living quarters.

seeThis.title: Cave 23's Buddhas

The numbering runs left to right along the scarp, so walk it in order rather than doubling back.
Carry water. There is nothing to buy once you are past the base of the hill.

story.tagline: The panel where a god lifts the earth out of the sea.
story.intro: Udayagiri is a low sandstone ridge a few kilometres from Vidisha in Madhya Pradesh, cut through with about twenty shrines and niches. It is one of the very few sites where Gupta-period sculpture survives in place rather than in a museum, and the dated inscriptions here are among the earliest firmly fixed points in Hindu temple art.
story.history: The caves belong mainly to the early fifth century, in the reign of Chandragupta II, whose court is recorded here in two inscriptions — one of them dated to 401–402 CE. Cave 5 holds the great relief of Vishnu as Varaha, the boar incarnation, hauling the earth-goddess out of the ocean while ranks of sages look on; it is usually read as a political image as much as a religious one, the king as the rescuer of the land. Other shrines are dedicated to Shiva, to Durga and to the Jain tirthankara Parshvanatha, whose cave carries a later inscription of 425–426 CE. The hill also holds cisterns, a ruined temple platform and a rock-cut passage aligned on the sunrise.

visiting.duration: Around two hours

seeThis.title: The Jain cave at the north end

The site has no shade and no shop; bring water and a hat.
Morning light falls straight into the Varaha panel, which is when it photographs best.

story.tagline: The stupa that held the bones of the Buddha's two chief disciples.
story.intro: Satdhara sits on a bluff above the Bes river about nine kilometres west of Sanchi, and it is the quietest of the group of Buddhist sites scattered around Vidisha. There are around thirty stupas here, a monastery and a temple platform, and for most of the year you will have the whole place to yourself.
story.history: The main stupa is broadly contemporary with Sanchi's — a hemispherical mound faced in dressed stone, begun in the second century BCE and enlarged later. Its importance is that in the 1850s Alexander Cunningham found in Stupa 2 relic caskets inscribed with the names of Sariputta and Moggallana, the Buddha's two principal disciples, matching the find made at Sanchi's Stupa 3. The caskets went to Britain in the nineteenth century, and relics from this group of sites were returned to India in the twentieth. The Archaeological Survey of India conserved and partly rebuilt the site in the 1990s.

story.tagline: The best-preserved capitals in the western Deccan, up ninety steps.
story.intro: Bedse is a small group of caves on a spur of the Sahyadris in Pune district's Maval taluka, above the village of Bedse. There are only a handful of excavations, but two of them are exceptional: a chaitya hall with a deep verandah, and a vihara built on an apsidal plan that is almost unique among the western Indian caves.
story.history: The caves belong to the first century BCE, making them roughly contemporary with Bhaja and a little earlier than Karla down the same valley. The chaitya is entered through a screen of four tall columns whose bell capitals carry pairs of animals with riders — horses, bulls and elephants — carved with a crispness that has survived far better here than at most comparable sites, because the verandah shelters them from the monsoon. Inside, twenty-four plain octagonal pillars run round a stone stupa. The neighbouring vihara is apsidal rather than square, with cells opening off a curved wall, a plan found almost nowhere else.

visiting.bestTime: June to February — the valley is greenest just after the monsoon
visiting.duration: An hour and a half, plus the climb

story.intro: Kondana is a group of sixteen Buddhist caves cut into a hillside near Kondhane village in Raigad district, on the old route up the ghats below Rajmachi. It is one of the least visited of the western Indian cave sites, largely because the only way in is a walk.
story.history: The excavations are early — first century BCE — and belong to the same phase of building as Bhaja and Bedse, when Buddhist communities settled beside the passes that carried trade from the Konkan coast up onto the Deccan. There is one chaitya hall and a group of viharas. The chaitya's facade is carved in imitation of a wooden building, down to the beam ends and the lattice of a great horseshoe window, and inside, the ribs of the vault were originally fitted with actual timber. Part of the facade collapsed after heavy rain in 2014 and has since been stabilised.

visiting.duration: An hour at the caves; allow half a day with the walk

story.tagline: A tower of granite in a delta made of mud.
story.intro: The Brihadeeswarar temple — the Peruvudaiyar Kovil, the Big Temple — was finished in about 1010 CE by the Chola emperor Rajaraja I, and it is still the largest thing in Thanjavur. Its vimana rises around sixty-six metres over the sanctum. UNESCO inscribed it in 1987 as the first of the Great Living Chola Temples; it has been in continuous worship for over a thousand years.
story.history: Rajaraja I built it at the height of Chola power, when the dynasty's fleets and armies reached Sri Lanka and beyond, and he paid for it out of that empire. The whole structure is granite — hundreds of thousands of tonnes of it — in a delta district where granite does not occur, so every block was hauled in. The inscriptions cut round the base are an administrative archive: they list the endowments, the dancers, the musicians, the accountants and the villages whose revenue kept the temple running. Inside the passage round the sanctum are Chola-period frescoes, painted over in the Nayaka period and only uncovered in the twentieth century. The Nandi facing the shrine is cut from a single block of stone.

story.tagline: Carved as though the stone were ivory.
story.intro: Airavatesvara at Darasuram, on the edge of Kumbakonam, is the third of the Great Living Chola Temples and by far the smallest. What it lacks in scale it makes up in detail: the mandapa is built as a chariot drawn by horses, and the friezes round it are cut at a size closer to jewellery than architecture.
story.history: It was built in the twelfth century under Rajaraja II, at a point when the Cholas had stopped competing on size and started competing on refinement. The temple is dedicated to Shiva as Airavatesvara — the lord worshipped by Airavata, Indra's white elephant. The front mandapa is shaped as a processional chariot on wheels, with stone horses at the front. Panels round the base run through the lives of the sixty-three Nayanmar saints in miniature. Some of the steps at the southern entrance are said to produce different notes when struck, which is why they are now roped off. UNESCO added it to the Great Living Chola Temples inscription in 2004.

story.tagline: The building the Taj Mahal is descended from.
story.intro: Humayun's tomb stands in a walled garden in Nizamuddin, east Delhi, and it is the first monumental Mughal tomb in India — the building that established the type the Taj Mahal would perfect eighty years later. It was inscribed by UNESCO in 1993.
story.history: Humayun, the second Mughal emperor, died in 1556. The tomb was commissioned by his widow Hamida Banu Begum and completed around 1571 to a design by the Persian architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas. It brought several things to India at once: the charbagh, a garden quartered by water channels; the high arched plinth; and the double dome, an outer shell for the skyline and an inner one scaled to the chamber below. Red sandstone with white marble inlay set the palette for Mughal building for a century. More than a hundred later Mughals were eventually buried in the chambers around the central hall. It was here that the last emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, was captured by British troops in 1857.

story.tagline: Nine doors, no altar, no sermon.
story.intro: The Baháʼí House of Worship at Bahapur in south Delhi is known to everybody as the Lotus Temple, because that is exactly what it looks like: twenty-seven marble-clad petals in clusters of three, forming nine sides with nine doors, set among nine pools. It opened in 1986 and is one of the most-visited buildings in the world.
story.history: It was designed by the Iranian-Canadian architect Fariborz Sahba and engineered by Flint & Neill, and took about six years to build. The Baháʼí faith requires its houses of worship to be nine-sided and open to people of every religion, so the plan follows that rule rather than any architectural fashion. The marble is Pentelic, from the same Greek quarries used for the Parthenon. Inside there is a single hall seating about 1,300 people, with no images, no pulpit and no ritual — scripture from any faith may be read or sung, but not accompanied by instruments. The building has collected a long list of engineering and architecture awards for the geometry of its shells.

visiting.hours: Tuesday to Sunday, closed Mondays; hours shorten in winter

story.tagline: The wall is so close to the cliff you cannot tell where the rock stops.
story.intro: Mehrangarh stands on a sandstone outcrop about 120 metres above Jodhpur, and the old city spreads out beneath it in the blue-washed houses that give it its nickname. The fort was begun in 1459 and has been held by the Rathore rulers of Marwar ever since; it is now run by a trust and is one of the best-kept fort museums in India. A kilometre away, the white marble cenotaph of Jaswant Thada sits above its own tank.
story.history: Rao Jodha moved his capital here from Mandore in 1459 and started the fort on the hill the locals called Bhaurcheeria, the mountain of birds. Most of what stands today is later — the great gates, the courtyards and the palaces were added between the seventeenth and nineteenth centuries. The gates still carry the handprints of royal widows who committed sati, and one, Jayapol, was built to mark a victory over the armies of Jaipur and Bikaner. Jaswant Thada was built in 1899 by Maharaja Sardar Singh for his father Jaswant Singh II, out of sheets of marble cut so thin that they glow when the sun is behind them.

visiting.duration: Half a day for both

story.tagline: Two brothers carved one half each, and never quite agreed.
story.intro: Nathmal ki Haveli stands in the lanes below Jaisalmer fort, one of the group of merchant mansions that make the town as interesting as its citadel. It is late-nineteenth-century, cut from the same honey-coloured sandstone as everything else here, and it has one famous quirk.
story.history: The haveli was built in the 1880s for Diwan Mohata Nathmal, the prime minister of Jaisalmer state. Two brothers, Hathi and Lulu, were commissioned to carve it, and they worked from opposite ends of the facade at the same time. The two halves are similar enough to read as one building and different enough that once you notice, you cannot stop looking — the brackets, the panels and the window screens do not match across the centre line. Elephants flank the entrance. Inside, some of the rooms keep their painted decoration, and parts of the building are still lived in.

visiting.duration: Half an hour to an hour

story.tagline: One of several hundred temples in a single square kilometre.
story.intro: Siddheswara stands in the Old Town of Bhubaneswar, immediately beside the better-known Mukteswara temple, in a district that once held several hundred shrines around the Bindusagar tank. It is a compact Kalinga-style temple — a curved tower over the sanctum and a pyramid-roofed hall in front — and unusually for the area it is still in worship and rarely crowded.
story.history: Bhubaneswar's Old Town was the religious centre of Kalinga from roughly the seventh to the thirteenth centuries, and the temples there record the whole development of the Odishan style over that period. Siddheswara belongs to the later part of that sequence. Its plan is the standard pair: a rekha deul, the tall curvilinear tower over the sanctum, and a jagamohana, the assembly hall, roofed as a stepped pyramid. A seated Ganesha occupies one of the outer niches. The temple sits within the walled compound it shares with Mukteswara, whose carved torana arch is the single most photographed thing in the Old Town.

story.tagline: Temples on a river that has almost dried up around them.
story.intro: The Prachi is a small river running east through Cuttack and Puri districts, and the villages along it hold a scatter of stone temples that almost nobody visits. Sobhaneswara at Niali and Gangeswari at Bayalisabati are two of the better preserved, and both stand more or less as they were left, in compounds shaded by old trees.
story.history: The valley was a settled religious landscape from around the ninth century onward, and its temples follow the Kalinga idiom of the Bhubaneswar workshops at a smaller scale. Sobhaneswara at Niali is a Shiva temple of the eleventh to twelfth centuries, with the usual pairing of curved sanctum tower and pyramidal hall. Gangeswari at Bayalisabati is best known for its sculpture rather than its architecture: a Saptamatrika panel, the seven mother goddesses in a row, and a Varahi image that scholars of Odishan sculpture cite regularly. Both sites are protected but lightly managed, and the Prachi itself now carries far less water than the settlements along it were built for.

visiting.duration: Half a day for both, including the driving

story.tagline: Where the tenth Guru dictated the scripture in full.
story.intro: Takht Sri Damdama Sahib stands at Talwandi Sabo in Bathinda district, in flat Malwa farmland a long way from anywhere. It is the fifth and most recently recognised of the Sikh Takhts — the five seats of temporal authority in Sikhism — and its importance is textual: this is where the final recension of the Guru Granth Sahib was dictated.
story.history: Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru, arrived here in 1705 after the battles at Chamkaur and Muktsar and stayed about nine months. During that stay he dictated the complete Guru Granth Sahib to Bhai Mani Singh, adding the compositions of the ninth Guru, Tegh Bahadur, to the volume compiled by Guru Arjan. The resulting text — the Damdama Sahib recension — is the one used ever since. Damdama means a resting place, and the Guru is said to have called it his Kashi, a seat of learning; the tradition of Sikh scriptural scholarship that grew here is still known as the Damdami Taksal. It was formally recognised as the fifth Takht in the twentieth century.

story.tagline: A walled city of pols, still being driven through every day.
story.intro: Ahmedabad's walled city was inscribed by UNESCO in 2017 as India's first World Heritage City. What is protected is not one monument but a fabric: six centuries of dense, layered urbanism — the pols, the fort quarter, the mosques, the wooden-fronted houses — still lived in and still moving. These vantages are street-level captures made from a vehicle, so what you get is the city as it is used rather than as it is posed.
story.history: Sultan Ahmad Shah I founded the city in 1411 on the east bank of the Sabarmati and built the Bhadra citadel at its centre. Under the Gujarat Sultanate it became one of the great trading cities of western India, and its architecture fused Islamic form with Gujarati carving traditions — the Jami Masjid, the Sidi Saiyyed screen, the stepwells. Behind the main streets the residential city was organised into pols: gated clusters of houses, usually of one community, with their own wells, bird-feeders and internal squares. The British period added mills, and the twentieth century added Gandhi's ashram upriver at Sabarmati. The old city's plan has survived all of it.

visiting.hours: Streets are public; monuments broadly sunrise to sunset
visiting.duration: A morning on foot for the core
